messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGMs to estimate network change
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users,

I have a question about whether ERGMs are appropriate to answer the question of whether similarity on a stable attribute can predict network change.  I know SIENA was developed for this purpose; however, for the purposes of a paper I am combining a longitudinal analysis with another analysis that is necessarily cross-sectional.  Because I am writing for a non-network audience I thought it would be more straightforward to use ERGMs for all of the analyses.

Here is the question: is it acceptable to estimate an ERGM that predicts the time 2 network and includes the following predictors: (1) attribute similarity at time 1, (2) the network at time 1 (as a dyadic covariate), and (3) structural effects for the time 2 network?  Would this approach tell me whether similarity on the attribute drives network change (assuming the attribute itself is constant over time)?

Here is the specific syntax:
model6 <- ergm(net2 ~ edges + edgecov(net1) + edgecov(activities) +
    nodematch("educ") + nodematch("sex") + nodematch("race") + nodematch("grade") +
    gwdegree(.25, fixed=TRUE) + gwdsp(.25, fixed=TRUE) + gwesp(.25, fixed=TRUE) )

Is this type of an ERGM approach justifiable in this situation?  Are there other tradeoffs between the two approaches that should be considered?  I have seen this approach used in at least one published piece, but I haven't seen a statistician's take on it.

I appreciate any insight on this issue.

Thanks,
David

***********************************

Assistant Professor
School of Social and Family Dynamics
Arizona State University

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

as part of its annual recruitment and selection procedure for 
PhD-students, the Interuniversity Center for Social Science Theory and 
Methodology (ICS) in the Netherlands is looking for excellent candidates 
for a couple of four-year-long PhD projects on several network-related 
topics. In particular, we are looking for candidates interested in the 
following projects in statistical network analysis:

    Project "Statistical Models for Three-Way Network Data"
    Examples of three-way social processes are gossip (where two people
    choose a third person, an ?object? to talk about), informal
    mediation (where a colleague might entrust a problem with another
    colleague to a third colleague, who acts as mediator to solve the
    problem), or social cognitive maps (where actors in a dyadic network
    report their perceptions of the whole network). While in dyadic
    network data actors have two roles, as 'sender' and 'receiver', in
    triadic observations they have a third role, for instance as
    'object' (of gossip), as 'mediator' (of problems with colleagues),
    or as 'observer' (of dyadic relations). While older work
    (Krackhardt, 1987) focused on how to summarize triadic data to
    obtain a dyadic network, such data reduction implies a potentially
    severe loss of information. So far, not much work has been done to
    develop statistical models for three-way data (see Bond & Kenny,
    2002, for an exception). This project focuses on the development of
    appropriate statistical models to handle the richness of this type
    of data.

    Project "Validity of Models for Network Structure and Social
    Influence Processes"
    In the past decade, the analysis of social networks with statistical
    models has developed rapidly with the availability of new estimation
    methods, using advanced computational techniques, coupled with new
    insights in the complex structure of social network data. On the one
    hand, these are models explaining the shape of networks as such,
    i.e., the interdependencies between the network actors. On the other
    hand, there are models using networks to explain other phenomena,
    such as (change in) status, performance, or peer influence. Many new
    methods and models have been proposed, one of them being stochastic
    actor-based modeling ("SIENA"), proposed by the project initiators.
    However, there are hardly any studies comparing the different
    approaches.As a consequence, the demarcation of the conclusions that
    can reliably be drawn with the available methods remains an open
    question and guidelines for the selection of appropriate analytical
    methods are lacking. This project aims to fill these gaps.

The two projects will be supervised by Christian Steglich, Marijtje van 
Duijn, Mark Huisman, and Tom Snijders. The recruitment and selection 
procedure for our scholarships starts December 11, 2010. Applications, 
online only, should be delivered through the ICS website before January 
15, 2011. The interviews will be conducted on March 3, 4, 8 and 9, 2011.

More details, also about the other available positions, can be found via 
the website http://www.ics-graduateschool.nl/vacancies/

We very much appreciate your interest and cooperation,

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Your question provoked a bit of discussion behind the curtain, so you 
may get more than one response.  In theory, yes, you should be able to do 
this.  My own guess is that estimation will be pretty unstable unless you 
have a lot of change from t1 to t2.

With respect to the interpretation of the paramters, I'm not sure this 
would be the right way to identify how nodal attributes drive network 
change.  That's because change has 2 components: formation and dissolution 
of ties.  There may be different dynamics driving the two factors, and 
they would be confounded in the approach you're taking.

best,
mm

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

When I try to estimate model for an undirected network with a large number of
dyads set as missing (NA), it returns me degenerate models.

In what I am working on, I need to set as NA the 20% of the dyads. I tried
with Lazega's Lawyers and Kapfter's tailor shop data.

These problems there were not until the version ergm 2.2-5, I think that
it is not a bug but a problem of the algorithm with low density network.

Attached find a toy example:




library(statnet)

###################

getDyad<-function(net){
n<-network.size(net)
pair<-NULL
if(is.directed(net)){
	for(i in 1:(n-1))for(j in (i+1):n) pair<-rbind(pair,c(i,j),c(j,i))
}
else{
	for(i in 1:(n-1))for(j in (i+1):n) pair<-rbind(pair,c(i,j))
}
return(pair)
}

###################################

#### low density

m <- matrix(rbinom(30^2,1,.07),30,30)
diag(m) <- 0
g <- network(m, directed=FALSE)
summary(g)
plot(g)



ERGMa1<-ergm(g~edges
#+gwdegree(.5,fixed=TRUE)
+gwesp(.5,fixed=TRUE)
#+gwdsp(0.25,fixed=TRUE)
,burnin=100000,interval=5000, MCMCsamplesize=10000,maxit=5)




summary(ERGMa1)
plot(ERGMa1)



coppie<-getDyad(g)

m<-dim(coppie)[1]

c<-sample(1:m,40)

prova<-g

prova[coppie[c,]]<-NA


ERGMa2<-ergm(prova~edges
#+gwdegree(.5,fixed=TRUE)
+gwesp(1,fixed=TRUE)
#+gwdsp(0.25,fixed=TRUE)
,burnin=100000,interval=5000, MCMCsamplesize=10000,maxit=5)


summary(ERGMa2)
plot(ERGMa2)


######### large density

m <- matrix(rbinom(30^2,1,.3),30,30)
diag(m) <- 0
g2 <- network(m, directed=FALSE)
summary(g2)
plot(g2)




ERGMb1<-ergm(g2~edges
#+gwdegree(.5,fixed=TRUE)
+gwesp(1,fixed=TRUE)
#+gwdsp(0.25,fixed=TRUE)
,burnin=100000,interval=5000, MCMCsamplesize=5000)


summary(ERGMb1)
plot(ERGMb1)


prova2<-g2

prova2[coppie[c,]]<-NA


ERGMb2<-ergm(prova2~edges
#+gwdegree(.5,fixed=TRUE)
+gwesp(1,fixed=TRUE)
#+gwdsp(0.25,fixed=TRUE)
,burnin=100000,interval=5000, MCMCsamplesize=5000)


summary(ERGMb2)
plot(ERGMb2)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] community detection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Moses,

This is an interesting question, one that is best answered by another: What is the scientific purpose of the community detection?

If the purpose is to find a categorization of the nodes into relatively homogeneous groups then any of the commonly used algorithms can achieve this. They can produce useful 
descriptives.

If the purpose is to detect underlying categorizations in the presence of stochastic variation, to test if such categorizations are real, to look at other categorizations that have 
support from the data, etc, then it is scientifically better to consider model-based approaches. This also allows to define communities adjusted for nodal and dyadic covariates, 
and to adjust for node specific heterogeneity, etc. We have taken this latter approach in "statnet".

In particular, I would point you toward "latentnet". It has a latent position cluster model that embeds the nodes within a latent social space and estimates 
clusters/communities/groups via a stochastic model. It incorporates the statistical uncertainty, especially uncertainty in the community identifications. It is a very visual model. 
One reference is <http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i05/paper> and a later paper in Social Networks.

There are other model-based approaches, but this is a start and well supported and developed in "statnet".

I hope this helps.

Cheers,

Mark
